body: Not as a metaphor. As a measured drug-reward response.
punch: And it showed up in adolescent animals specifically.

headline: Nobody frames these
body: The discussion is always about physical risk — liver, heart, hormones. Dependence potential barely enters the conversation.
punch: Which is odd, because it was tested directly.

headline: The test
body: Animals learn to associate a location with a drug. If they then choose to spend time there, the drug was rewarding. It's a standard measure of abuse potential.
punch: A behavioural readout for wanting more.

headline: Nandrolone
body: In adolescent male mice — not only adults. The compound registered as rewarding in animals at the developmental stage that matters most here.
punch: The age group using these is the age group it acted on.

headline: And there was
body: Altered D1 dopamine receptor expression in the nucleus accumbens — the core reward structure. So the behaviour came with a matching change in the circuit.
punch: Behaviour and biology pointing the same direction.

headline: Why this matters
body: A compound with reward properties is one people continue past their original intention. That changes the risk calculus from a single decision into a repeated one.
punch: Dose creep isn't a character flaw. It's pharmacology.

headline: It also reframes
body: Telling someone to run a short conservative course assumes the decision to stop is purely rational. Reward pathways are specifically the thing that makes stopping harder.
punch: The plan assumes a brain the drug is acting on.

headline: The limits
body: Mouse behavioural work. Conditioned place preference indicates reward, not clinical addiction, and rodent dosing isn't human use.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
